sources_considered.why: Survey of nearly 400 lawyers fielded Nov 2024 to Jan 2025 on generative AI use.
LA Times column on lawyer hallucination cases in 2025 and how unaware the lawyers seemed.
Covers the May 2025 Utah sanction. Not used: it reports the lawyer was unaware ChatGPT had been used at all, which is not quite shock at fabrication, and the article date is unclear.

evidence_items.locator: Section 'A Look at Legal AI's Uses'

receipt.public_excerpt: Legal research is the most common area of application today, with 40% of respondents using generative AI for that purpose.

evidence_items.explanation: A survey of nearly 400 lawyers, fielded through early January 2025, found that 40% used generative AI for legal research and more than a quarter used it for document creation. That supports 'a lot of lawyers' using such tools for brief preparation.

evidence_items.locator: Paragraph beginning 'In most of the cases'

receipt.public_excerpt: in some 30 cases involving lawyers the AI-generated errors were discovered or were in documents filed as recently as this year, long after the tendency of AI bots to "hallucinate" became evident.

evidence_items.explanation: About 30 lawyer cases with AI-generated errors had been found in 2025 alone, long after the risk was widely known. This fits 'many still' being caught out.

receipt.public_excerpt: It's peopled by lawyers who appear to be totally oblivious to the technological world they live in.

evidence_items.explanation: A contemporary journalist describes the lawyers in these cases as apparently oblivious, which matches Marcus's impression that many 'seem shocked'.

unresolved_gaps: No source directly measures how many lawyers were 'shocked'. That part rests on journalists' and judges' descriptions.
The survey covers generative AI in general, not ChatGPT specifically, and does not break out brief-writing as a category.
